blocks.prompt: The Bird With a Flag on Its Head
blocks.text: Most parrots are bright green and blue. The cockatoo is not. Cockatoos are white, black, gray, or soft pink. But a cockatoo has one thing other parrots do not have. It has a crest of long feathers on top of its head. It can raise the crest or lower it whenever it wants. A calm cockatoo keeps its crest folded down. A surprised cockatoo throws its crest straight up. Other cockatoos can see that from far away. Cockatoos live in Australia and on the islands nearby. They fly in big noisy flocks. While the flock eats seeds on the ground, one bird sits up in a tree and watches. If it sees a cat or a hawk, it screeches, and the whole flock jumps into the sky.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Raises a Flag
blocks.text: Every cockatoo carries a flag on its head. The flag is made of feathers, and it is called a crest. Most parrots have smooth, flat heads. A cockatoo can snap its crest straight up or fold it down flat, and it chooses when to do it. The crest goes up when the bird is startled, when it is angry, and when it is showing off. The crest stays down when the bird is calm. Other cockatoos read that flag from clear across the treetops, which is useful when your flock is spread through a whole stand of trees. There is a second difference. Most parrots glow in green and blue. Cockatoos never do. Their feathers are missing the tiny structure that bends light into those shades, so cockatoos come in white, black, gray, and pink instead. What they gave up in color they made up for in volume. A flock of cockatoos screeching in a gum tree can be heard a mile away. Cockatoos live in Australia, New Guinea, and the islands around them, and some of them live a very long time. A cockatoo named Cookie lived at a zoo in Illinois until he was eighty-three years old.

blocks.prompt: The Trick That Traveled
blocks.text: In 2018, people in a few suburbs of Sydney, Australia, started finding their trash pulled across the driveway every week. The culprits were not raccoons or dogs. They were sulphur-crested cockatoos, big white parrots with yellow crests, and they had worked out how to open a wheeled trash bin. It is not a simple job. The bird has to pry the lid up with its beak, walk its beak along the rim while holding the lid open, then flip the whole lid over backward before it drops shut. Then it climbs in and eats. Scientists wanted to know whether every cockatoo had invented this on its own. So they asked people all over Sydney to report bin-opening birds, and they marked individual cockatoos with paint dots so they could follow them. The answer was clear. The trick was not being invented over and over. It was spreading. It started in three suburbs. Two years later, cockatoos were opening bins in forty-four of them, and the trick moved outward from each starting point like a ripple, suburb by neighboring suburb. Birds were watching other birds and copying what worked. Even stranger, cockatoos in different areas opened their bins in slightly different styles, the way people in different places speak with different accents. Scientists have a word for behavior that is learned from your neighbors and passed along rather than born into you. That word is culture. Most of us assume culture belongs to humans. A parrot in a driveway suggests otherwise.

blocks.prompt: The Drummer in the Rainforest
blocks.text: Deep in the rainforest of far northern Australia lives a bird that makes music with a tool. The palm cockatoo is enormous, sooty black, with a bare red cheek that flushes brighter when the bird is worked up. In breeding season, a male finds a dead branch. He does not simply grab it. He breaks it to length, strips it, and trims it until it is the shape he wants. Then he takes his manufactured drumstick in one foot, chooses a hollow trunk, and beats out a rhythm you can hear across the valley. Researchers recorded these performances for years and found something they did not expect. The drumming is not random banging. Each male keeps a steady beat, and each male has his own signature rhythm, distinct enough that you can tell one bird from another by listening. Outside of humans, that combination of making a tool and using it to keep time is close to unheard of. The palm cockatoo is not the only member of the family bending objects to its purpose. In a laboratory in Austria, a Goffin's cockatoo named Figaro was given a nut placed out of reach behind a barrier. Nobody taught him what to do. He tore a long splinter from a wooden beam, shaped it, reached through the gap, and raked the nut in. Then he did it again with fresh materials, and the other cockatoos in his aviary watched him and started doing it too. Wild Goffin's cockatoos have since been found making toolkits of two and three different tools to open a fruit, carrying the set from tree to tree. So when Sydney's sulphur-crested cockatoos taught one another to flip open wheeled trash bins, and the trick rippled from three suburbs to forty-four in two years, it should not have been a shock. Cockatoos have long lives, and a long childhood, and a flock full of other cockatoos to watch. That is the recipe for learning. The bins were simply the newest puzzle we happened to leave in the driveway.

blocks.prompt: An Arms Race in the Driveway
blocks.text: The cockatoos of Australia are, by most measures, a family that gave things up. There are about twenty-one species, and almost none of them wear the electric greens and blues that make other parrots famous. Those shades are not paint. They are a trick of architecture: a microscopic feather structure that scatters light into blue, which then passes through a yellow pigment and emerges green. Cockatoo feathers lack that structure entirely. What is left is white, black, gray, and a few soft pinks. In exchange, the family kept two things. The first is the crest, a fan of feathers that a cockatoo raises and lowers deliberately, a mood broadcast legible to every other bird in the canopy. The second is a brain that will not leave a puzzle alone. Consider the palm cockatoo of the far north. In breeding season a male selects a dead branch, snaps it to length, strips and trims it into a drumstick, grips it in one foot, and beats a rhythm against a hollow trunk. Researchers who recorded these performances over seven years found that the beats were regular and that each male drummed a pattern of his own, consistent enough to identify him by ear. Manufacturing an object in order to keep time is a description that, until recently, applied to exactly one species on this planet. Consider Figaro, a Goffin's cockatoo in an Austrian laboratory, handed a nut placed deliberately out of reach. Untaught, he tore a splinter from a wooden beam, worked it into a rake, and drew the nut in. His flockmates watched and learned. Wild Goffin's have since been observed assembling sets of two or three distinct tools to open a single fruit and carrying the kit between trees, which means the bird is not solving the problem in front of it. It is anticipating the problem ahead of it. Which brings us to the driveways of Sydney. Around 2018, sulphur-crested cockatoos began opening household trash bins: prying the lid, walking the beak along the rim while bracing it open, then flipping the lid backward. Scientists recruited thousands of residents to report sightings and paint-marked individual birds to follow them. The trick had begun in three suburbs. Within two years it was being performed in forty-four, spreading outward neighbor to neighbor, and birds in different districts had settled into different opening styles. This is the technical definition of culture: behavior invented by an individual, transmitted socially, and varying by region. What happened next is the part people miss. Residents fought back. They weighted the lids with bricks, jammed sticks into the hinges, bolted them shut. The cockatoos worked around the bricks. The residents escalated. Researchers now describe the situation as an innovation arms race, and they are careful to note that only one side has been formally studied. It is tempting to file all of this under clever animal. That would be a mistake, and the reason is chronological. Cockatoos were prying open the seed cases of this continent for millions of years before anyone rolled a plastic bin onto a curb. The bin is not the achievement. The bin is a seed case we invented, put in their territory, and filled with food. A bird that solves your bin is a bird that was always solving something.
